vessel.label: vessel radius
vessel.note: Half the lumen diameter of the small arteries whose wall tension was measured. Perforators below 0.5 mm are small arteries in Mulvany's sense (mulvany1990).

vessel.label: maximal active wall tension
vessel.quote: the maximal active tension of arteries (3.4 +/- 0.42 mN/mm)
vessel.note: Maximal active wall tension (1 mN/mm = 1 N/m); the range is ± 2 SE. Rat mesenteric small arteries.

vessel.label: stretch of greatest force
vessel.quote: The arteries were then set to the 90% of the determined internal circumference under a transmural pressure of 100 mmHg (L 100 ), at which point the force development was close to maximal.
vessel.note: Human small arteries develop their greatest active force near 0.9 of the relaxed circumference at 100 mmHg; the same sentence defines r100.

vessel.label: pressure inside the vessel
vessel.quote: The microvascular pressure in arterioles of 70 mum in diameter or larger was proportional to the systemic arterial pressure (PA).
vessel.note: Pressure inside the perforator. Small arteries lie upstream of the main resistance (the 20–35 µm arterioles), so their pressure is a large fraction of arterial pressure; results are shown across the whole range.

vessel.label: stiffness of the relaxed wall
vessel.note: Stiffness of the relaxed wall (passive tension rises as exp(β·(x − 1))). To be sourced from pressure-myograph curves.

vessel.label: width of the length–tension curve
vessel.note: Width of the active length–tension curve, as a fraction of the optimal muscle length.

vessel.label: thickness of the wall
vessel.note: Cross-sectional area of the media, in units of r100²; a media thickness of 5–10% of the lumen diameter. Sets how short the muscle becomes when the lumen closes.

vessel.label: shut radius
vessel.note: Lumen radius at which the vessel is shut to flow; flow scales as radius⁴, so flow here is under 0.1% of rest.

vessel.label: speed of the wall
vessel.note: How fast the wall moves to its mechanical balance.

vessel.label: latency of the gasp reflex
vessel.quote: The median latency, measured from the start of the IG to the onset of the vasoconstriction, was reported as 3.6-3.8 seconds with no difference between genders, and the time to the minimum LDF value was 4.6-5.2 seconds, depending on the hand measured and gender
vessel.note: Delay between a deep inspiratory gasp and the constriction of skin vessels.

vessel.label: rise of tone
vessel.quote: The median latency, measured from the start of the IG to the onset of the vasoconstriction, was reported as 3.6-3.8 seconds with no difference between genders, and the time to the minimum LDF value was 4.6-5.2 seconds, depending on the hand measured and gender
vessel.note: Tone rises fast; flow reaches its minimum 1.0–1.4 s after the constriction begins.

vessel.label: fade of nerve-driven tone
vessel.quote: The overall duration of the reflex to recovery in this image is approximately 34 seconds, with the interval of near-zero LDF at approximately 10 seconds
vessel.fit: a gasp's constriction recovers (flow back to 95%) about 34 s after the gasp
vessel.note: How slowly nerve-driven tone fades once the drive stops (transmitter clearance and muscle relaxation). Fitted to one subject's recovery; to be refined with more recordings.

vessel.label: the gasp's burst
vessel.quote: The median latency, measured from the start of the IG to the onset of the vasoconstriction, was reported as 3.6-3.8 seconds with no difference between genders, and the time to the minimum LDF value was 4.6-5.2 seconds, depending on the hand measured and gender
vessel.note: A gasp's burst of sympathetic firing is brief: flow is lowest 1.0–1.4 s after the constriction begins.

vessel.label: fall in flow after a gasp
vessel.quote: the index of vasoconstrictor response (per cent change) induced by inspiratory gasp was higher in young males than in young females (71.4% versus 59.4%; P < 0.05)
vessel.note: Fall in fingertip skin blood flow after a deep gasp; the model sets the gasp's drive so an open vessel loses this share of its flow. Hairy skin, where most knots are, may respond less.

vessel.label: size of reactive hyperaemia
vessel.note: Rise of forearm skin perfusion from baseline to the peak of reactive hyperaemia. Sets resting tone, since a fully relaxed vessel must carry 2.87 times resting flow.

vessel.label: timing of reactive hyperaemia
vessel.note: Time from release of an occlusion to peak perfusion (± 1 SD). The model's flush is checked against it.

vessel.label: build-up of oxygen debt
vessel.note: How fast an unsupplied patch runs up an oxygen debt that its sensory nerves sense.

vessel.label: speed of the sensory nerves
vessel.fit: reactive hyperaemia peaks at porh_peak_time after a 5 min occlusion
vessel.note: How fast the sensory nerves release their dilator when blood returns to a patch in debt (sensory nerves and BKCa channels carry the skin's reactive hyperaemia, lorenzo2007). The dilator relaxes the muscle directly. Fitted so the flush peaks when the measured one does.

vessel.label: share supplied by neighbours
vessel.quote: Each perforasome is linked with adjacent perforasomes by means of two main mechanisms that include both direct and indirect linking vessels.
vessel.note: Share of a shut perforator's territory that neighbours keep supplied through linking vessels. The linking is measured; the share is a guess.

vessel.label: myogenic relaxation under pressure
vessel.quote: investigation of the vasoconstrictor response to raised intravascular pressure (the Bayliss response)
vessel.note: How much tone a small artery gives up when its transmural pressure is taken away (the Bayliss response run backwards). The response is established; its size here is a guess.

vessel.label: timing of myogenic relaxation
vessel.note: How long the myogenic relaxation takes under sustained pressure.

vessel.label: breath's swing in tone
vessel.note: How much ordinary slow breathing swings tone (a fraction of maximal activation), rising on the in-breath and falling on the out-breath.

checks.label: hyaluronan over trapezius and deltoid
checks.quote: 6 μg g-1 in the fascia overlying the trapezius and deltoid muscles
checks.note: Hyaluronan in the fascia over trapezius and deltoid, where knots are commonly reported.

checks.label: hyaluronan in the retinacula
checks.quote: In the fascia that surrounds joints, the hyaluronan increases to 90 μg g-1
checks.note: The richest fascia measured, the retinacula of the ankle.

checks.label: hyaluronan does not gel
checks.quote: There is no evidence of intermolecule hydrogen bonding causing gel formation in NaHA solutions without protein present.
checks.note: Hyaluronan alone, under physiological conditions, is a liquid, not a gel.

checks.label: viscosity of synovial fluid
checks.quote: The observed zero shear rate viscosity for synovial fluid from a healthy joint ranges from 1 to 175 Pa s
checks.note: Healthy synovial fluid holds milligrams of hyaluronan per millilitre, tens to hundreds of times the fascia's; its viscosity is an upper bound for any collar.

checks.label: hyaluronan in synovial fluid
checks.quote: The mean HA concentration was 3.4+/-0.6 mg/ml.
checks.note: Hyaluronan in normal knee joint fluid, the source of the viscosity bound (eta_max); roughly 40–570 times the fascia's.

checks.label: thickness of the collar
checks.note: Thickness of the hyaluronan-rich layer around the vessel where it passes through the fascia. A thinner collar shears faster, so the low end is the collar's best case.

checks.label: radiative heat loss
checks.quote: The radiative heat transfer coefficient measured for the whole-body was 4.5 W/m2 per K for both the seated and standing cases
checks.note: Heat lost from the skin by radiation, per degree.

checks.label: convective heat loss
checks.quote: the whole-body natural convection coefficient for the manikin fell within the mid-range of previously published values at 3.4 and 3.3 W/m2 per K when standing and seated respectively
checks.note: Heat lost from the skin by convection in still air, per degree.

checks.label: maximal skin blood flow
checks.quote: skin blood flow can reach 6 to 8 L/min during hyperthermia
checks.note: Whole-body skin blood flow at its maximum; the fastest a patch can be warmed from within.

checks.label: skin area
checks.note: Skin area of an adult, to turn whole-body flow into flow per square metre.

checks.label: heat capacity of tissue
checks.note: Volumetric heat capacity of skin and subcutis, which are mostly water (water is 4.2e6).

checks.label: heat capacity of blood
checks.note: Volumetric heat capacity of blood.

checks.label: depth of the warmed layer
checks.note: Depth of skin and superficial fat whose temperature a perforator's flow sets.

checks.label: the latch, in the model
checks.quote: Comparison of the rate constants indicates that latch-bridge detachment is the rate-limiting step.
checks.note: In the latch-bridge model, force is lost at the pace of latch-bridge detachment.

checks.label: the latch, in tissue
checks.quote: The rate-limiting step for relaxation appears to be removal of [Ca2+] and not latch-bridge detachment.
checks.note: In arterial tissue, relaxation follows the fall of calcium; the latch does not hold force on its own.

checks.label: the latch's economy
checks.quote: In sustained contractions, Ca2+, cross-bridge phosphorylation, and ATP consumption rates fall, a phenomenon termed "latch".
checks.note: What the latch buys is economy: force held with less calcium and less ATP.

checks.label: age and adrenergic drive
checks.quote: The inhibition of STIM/Orai with YM-58483 (20 μM) reversed adrenergic hypercontractility in MA from older subjects
checks.note: Human small arteries from older donors contract more to adrenergic drive, one route by which age could push vessels into the switch's window.

checks.label: arterioles held shut by nerves
checks.quote: Following denervation, a 22.2 +/- 6.3% (SE) and 61.8 +/- 12 increase in the number of third-order arterioles open to flow occurred in WKY and SHR.
checks.note: Nerves hold some arterioles shut in living tissue; cut them and more open.

checks.label: the closing threshold
checks.quote: When pressure in an arteriole falls below its critical closing pressure (CCP), the smooth muscle generates enough wall tension to snap the vessel shut.
checks.note: The switch itself, as clinical physiology describes it.

checks.label: staying shut
checks.quote: it falls abruptly towards zero and remains minimal until pressure rises above the CCP threshold
checks.note: Once shut, a vessel stays shut until the balance tips back.

checks.label: the threshold in skin
checks.quote: Results demonstrate that a relatively high intraarterial pressure must be applied to this skin flap before blood flow will commence.
checks.note: The same threshold, measured in skin.

fitted.target: the fall in fingertip flow after a deep gasp (gasp_drop)
the recovery of flow about 34 s after a gasp
